scenes.name: Country-rock y roots-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En los setenta, el reajuste a los viejos valores (blues, folk, country) convierte al rock en uno de los mayores éxitos del consumismo: el Establishment ya no intenta destruirlo, lo absorbe. El country-rock de Gram Parsons es una moda enorme: Commander Cody, New Riders Of The Purple Sage, Manassas, Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, Poco y los Eagles (Desperado, Hotel California); en Nashville surgen los «outlaws» (Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Kris Kristofferson). El roots-rock sigue con Hot Tuna, Little Feat y Doobie Brothers, y la nostalgia recupera el blues (Roy Buchanan, Bonnie Raitt), la armonía vocal (Manhattan Transfer, Roches, McGarrigle Sisters) y los cincuenta (American Graffiti).

podcast.body: In a 1974 Rolling Stone interview, Don Henley expressed the band's desire to move beyond the country rock label and "ballad syndrome," stating, "we like to be a nice little country rock band from Los Angeles about half the time we wanted to get away from the ballad syndrome." "we like to be a nice little country rock band from Los Angeles about half the time we wanted to get away from the ballad syndrome."

podcast.title: Band Dynamics and Industry Fatigue (1979)
podcast.body: By 1979, the Eagles were reportedly "sick of each other and sick of the music industry," a sentiment that likely contributed to "The Long Run" being seen as their final album. Critics also often viewed the band as "too corporate." "In 1979, the Eagles was a band that was sick of each other and sick of the music industry."

podcast.title: Musical Influences and Sound Philosophy (Glenn Frey, 1980)
podcast.body: Glenn Frey noted in 1980 that The Eagles aimed to combine the vocal strengths of Poco with the "toughness" of The Flying Burrito Brothers, as neither predecessor band possessed both qualities. "Glenn Fry said that the eagles borrowed a bit from the burrito brothers and a bit from polko... polko was a good band vocally but they didn't have much toughness the burrito brothers had the toughness but they weren't that good a band vocally so we kind of wanted to combine both of those elements."

podcast.body: Rusty Young observed that The Eagles succeeded commercially because their music could be played on both AM and country radio, indicating they "made commercial music" and "figured out what they had to leave out," which was likely the overt country elements. "the difference between picking up the pieces by polko and what the Eagles did is that the Eagles could be played on AM and country radio and polko could not."

podcast.body: In the 1970s, The Eagles rarely charted country, with major hits like "Take It Easy," "Desperado," and "Best of My Love" failing to touch the country charts. Their only top 10 country hit during their entire active period was the "very twangy" "Lyin' Eyes," which peaked at number eight country. "the Eagles almost never charted country. podcast.title: Post-Hotel California Pressures
podcast.body: By 1978, the Eagles were immensely popular following the success of "Hotel California" a year prior. However, their record label was growing impatient for a follow-up album. To manage expectations and alleviate the band's own monotony and stress from being months behind on their main project, they decided to record a Christmas song, which ultimately became their cover of "Please Come Home for Christmas." "Hotel California had cemented their status as superstars a year earlier, but their record label was getting a bit impatient waiting for the follow-up."

xref.body: Co-founded in 1998 by Josh Homme and Jesse Hughes, the band's name arose from a night spent listening to the Polish metal band Vader, leading someone to suggest playing "Death Metal, but like the Eagles." An alternative account states Josh Homme coined the phrase after someone in a bar mistakenly referred to Scorpions' "Winds of Change" as "Death Metal." "The name came from a night listening to a Polish metal band called Vader. And someone, no one is sure who, said, we should play Death Metal, but like the Eagles."

xref.title: Bataclan Attack (November 13, 2015)
xref.body: Josh Homme was not present at the Bataclan theater in Paris on November 13, 2015, when terrorists attacked an Eagles of Death Metal concert, resulting in the deaths of 89 people, due to his flexible touring schedule with the band. "That's why he wasn't at the Bataclan theater in Paris when terrorists took over the place on November 13th, 2015 and killed 89 people who were all at an Eagles of Deathmale show."

xref.title: Bataclan Terrorist Attack (November 13, 2015)
xref.body: On November 13, 2015, a sold-out Eagles of Death Metal concert at the Bataclan in Paris, attended by about 1500 people, became the target of a terrorist attack. Three gunmen, dressed in black and wearing suicide vests, entered the venue at 9:49 PM, after shooting people outside, and opened fire with AK-47s into the general admission area during the guitar solo of "I Love the Devil," plunging the hall into chaos with muzzle flashes as the only light. "One of the most shocking terrorist attacks to ever hit Europe happened at a concert on November 13, 2015 at a Paris venue called the Bataclan."

xref.title: Return to Paris After Attack (2016)
xref.body: Following the horrific Bataclan Massacre, Eagles of Death Metal defiantly returned to Paris on February 16, 2016. The band performed again in the city to finish their interrupted show and to pay tribute to the 90 victims, including their merchandise manager, Nick Alexander, who died in the attack. "On February 16, 2016, the band returned to Paris to finish the show and to pay tribute to those who died, including the group's merch manager, Nick Alexander."

xref.title: Bataclan Massacre Eyewitness Account
xref.body: Jesse Hughes, the singer for Eagles of Death Metal, provided a powerful account of what he witnessed from the stage during the Bataclan Massacre on November 13, 2015. He recounted seeing acts of immense bravery, with people shielding loved ones from bullets, rather than any cowardice. This quote underlines the tragic heroism amidst the terror. "I didn't just see people getting murdered. I saw people jump up and jump in front of bullets for the ones they love and give their life. I never saw a single coward that night. I only saw bravery."

xref.title: End of Siege and Casualties
xref.body: At 12:18 AM, the order was given to storm the gunmen, an operation that lasted three minutes. One gunman detonated a suicide belt, and the second was shot before he could detonate his. In total, 89 people died, including Eagles of Death Metal's tour manager. The trial for 20 men charged with plotting the various attacks, including at the Bataclan, concluded in 2022. "In the end, 89 people died, including the Eagles of Death Metal tour manager."

xref.title: Fake Live Recording Revelation
xref.body: An alleged live recording of Oasis was revealed by Noel Gallagher in 1997 to be a fake. The actual recording was from a sound check for a Sony convention at the Glen Eagles Hotel in 1993, where the band members were very drunk. They decided to falsely attribute the recording to "Dunning Glasgow" for a cooler image, as the Sony convention was deemed "not cool." The true origin was eventually noted on "The Masterplan" album, and the crowd noise was lifted from a T. Rex bootleg from The Roundhouse around 1973. "It's not from McGee at all. It's actually from a, we got invited to play a Sony convention just before we signed to creation because I think at the time Sony were bankrolling creation and I think they were able to have a look at us."

xref.title: Falsified Live Recording of "I Am the Walrus"
xref.body: The alleged live recording of "I Am the Walrus" released on the 1994 *Cigarettes & Alcohol* EP was later exposed as a fabrication. It was not recorded live at the Cat House in Glasgow in June 1994 as claimed, but rather during a drunken sound check for a Sony convention at the Glen Eagles Hotel in 1993. The band intentionally misrepresented its origin to enhance their image, even incorporating crowd noise taken from a 1973 Eric Clapton/Faces bootleg.

xref.title: Past Royalty Income as Retirement Annuity
xref.body: In the "old days," groups like The Eagles could effectively retire because they reliably received large royalty checks every six months from sales of records they had released decades earlier. "And groups like the Eagles and Fleetwood Mac could retire because every six months or so. A big fat royalty check would arrive in the mail as the result of sales of records that they released decades earlier."
